rows.verified: Rosin or colophony contained in solder flux can produce fume associated with serious respiratory illness.
Without effective control, solder fume rises into the breathing zone during manual soldering.
Intermittent soldering can create high short-term exposures, especially in enclosed spaces or awkward working positions.
HSE identifies rosin-based solder flux fume as a major cause of occupational asthma.
After solder-fume asthma is established, the effects may be permanent and very small further exposures can trigger attacks.
COSHH requires a suitable assessment and prevention or adequate control of exposure to rosin-based solder flux fume.
Control options include substituting non-rosin flux where possible, avoiding overheating, using effective extraction and keeping the head out of the fume plume.
Extraction systems require regular maintenance and exposed workers require appropriate health surveillance.
Solder-fume risk depends on flux chemistry, iron temperature, work duration, enclosure, worker position, extraction performance and sensitisation.
Solder-fume evidence is material-, task-, exposure- and worker-specific and is not an exact parcel-level asthma probability.
Optical radiation covers ultraviolet, visible and infrared radiation.
Ultraviolet exposure can damage the cornea and can cause skin reddening, burns, premature ageing and skin cancer.
High-power lasers can cause severe eye injury including blindness and can also burn skin.
The Artificial Optical Radiation at Work Regulations require protection from hazardous artificial optical-radiation sources.
Dutyholders using hazardous artificial optical sources must reduce associated risks as low as reasonably practicable.
Maintenance that exposes embedded higher-class lasers should be limited to trained and authorised personnel.
Protective eyewear decisions for open-beam laser work should follow the risk assessment and laser class.
Projector safety procedures should prevent staring into the beam and minimise standing in the beam while facing the projector.
Optical-radiation risk depends on wavelength, source power, beam class, exposure duration, distance, access controls, shielding and eye or skin protection.
Optical-radiation evidence is source-, task-, exposure- and person-specific and is not an exact parcel-level eye or skin-injury probability.
